rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham prayed for Ishmael alone; Isaac was not prayed for but was granted as a reward for Ishmael’s sacrifice.
rows.anchor: he was the sole child of Abraham (sws) for which he prayed to God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The succeeding sacrifice is Ishmael’s, not Isaac’s; the author says Farāhī exposed Jewish interpolations in Fī man huwa al-dhabīh.
rows.anchor: The succeeding verses mention his sacrifice and Abraham (sws) sacrificed him and not Isaac (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The descriptor ḥalīm signals Ishmael’s steadfast fortitude before his father’s knife, leading to the descriptions true to promises, patient, and steadfast.
rows.anchor: This quality signifies his steadfastness and fortitude that he showed before the knife of his father.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an also calls Abraham ḥalīm; Ishmael was the most prominent manifestation of his father’s qualities.
rows.anchor: the Qur’ān mentions precisely the same quality of میِلَحٌ for Abraham (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word saʿy refers to the age when a child begins to walk and run about.
rows.anchor: The word يْعَس refers to the age in which a child starts to run and walk about.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dream came when Ishmael had reached the age of walking about with and helping his father.
rows.anchor: when the son entered the age of walking and running about his father, a dream was seen by his father.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Torah places Ishmael at thirteen, an age when a son is especially beloved to his father, making the test exceptionally hard.
rows.anchor: It is evident from the Torah that at that time he was thirteen years old.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faithful devotion to God requires readiness to sacrifice what one loves most for God’s cause.
rows.anchor: no person can be truly perfect in his faithfulness to God unless he is ready

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although a dream needs interpretation and Abraham could have interpreted it, he chose to obey what he had seen directly.
rows.anchor: what is said in a dream needs to be interpreted and if Abraham (sws) wanted he could have interpreted this dream

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham saw the dream repeatedly: the present-tense wording fits recurrence, whereas a single occurrence would have used a past-tense form.
rows.anchor: Had he seen it just once the words يِف ِامَنَمْال ُتْیَأَُر were more appropriate.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham first assessed his son’s courage by explaining the dream and asking his opinion, trusting Ishmael’s intellect to reach the right decision.
rows.anchor: the first step that he took in this regard was to assess the courage of his son.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ishmael understood the dream as God’s directive rather than a mere vision and readily accepted it, trusting God to make him steadfast.
rows.anchor: Ishmael (sws) understood this dream to be a directive of God and not a mere vision

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When both submitted to God, Abraham prepared to slaughter his son and Ishmael submitted himself for sacrifice.
rows.anchor: both the father and the son got ready for the test.

rows.speaker: Some people
rows.claim: Some explain the forehead posture as a way for Abraham to avoid eye contact and prevent sympathy from impeding the slaughter.
rows.anchor: Some people are of the opinion that Abraham (sws) took this measure to avoid eye-contact with his beloved son while slaughtering

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the eye-contact explanation: a father prepared to sacrifice his only beloved son needed no such reassurance.
rows.anchor: A father who is prepared to slaughter his sole and beloved son does not need such assurances.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham laid Ishmael on his forehead to sacrifice him in prostration, the posture closest to God in Islam.
rows.anchor: The posture of prostration is the most likeable in Islam viz a viz proximity to God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording indicates that Abraham laid Ishmael prostrate on his forehead.
rows.anchor: The words imply that the father prostrated his son before him on his forehead.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As Abraham was about to slaughter Ishmael, God declared the dream fulfilled and made his success a reward for fitting conduct and sincerity.
rows.anchor: the success he has achieved in this trial is a reward of his befitting behaviour and sincere attitude.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dream’s purpose was to direct Abraham to dedicate his son to God’s service, not to kill him; becoming ready to sacrifice fulfilled it.
rows.anchor: the purpose of this dream shown to Abraham (sws) was to ask him to dedicate his son to the service of God

rows.speaker: People who have inferred from this
rows.claim: Some infer that God abrogated His directive before it was carried out.
rows.anchor: People who have inferred from this that the Almighty abrogated His own directive before it was carried out

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the abrogation inference as unwarranted because the correct interpretation makes further refutation unnecessary.
rows.anchor: In the wake of the correct interpretation of the verse, refutation of this view is not needed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who fulfill God’s directives properly receive great success in trials and Paradise; religious escapism weakens their capacity for divine trials and closes the way to success in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: people who try to fulfill all the directives of God in a befitting manner

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God calls this a great trial, and Abraham passed it in a manner that earned divine praise.
rows.anchor: the trial was not trivial; it was a great one. Abraham (sws) came out of it in flying colours.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because God says Abraham fulfilled the dream, Islahi concludes no greater earthly trial or success occurred.
rows.anchor: no greater a trial ever took place on this earth and no greater a success was achieved by anyone than Abraham (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God ransomed Ishmael by directing Abraham to slaughter a ram in his place.
rows.anchor: the Almighty directed Abraham (sws) to slaughter a ram in place of his son

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ram sacrifice became an enduring ritual of ḥajj, offered from Abraham’s time through the Day of Judgment.
rows.anchor: It is this sacrifice which by being included in the rituals of h@ajj is being continuously offered from the times of Abraham (sws) till today

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Animal sacrifice occurs across ancient religions from Adam, but none has the Abrahamic sacrifice’s significant universal status.
rows.anchor: no sacrifice has assumed such significant and universal status as this Abrahamic sacrifice.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated notice of later generations preserving Abraham’s way fulfills his prayer for lasting remembrance, granting him unparalleled eternal fame.
rows.anchor: The Almighty accepted this prayer and granted him eternal fame that stands unparalleled in history.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The peace formula is an independent prayer for Abraham’s peace and blessings in both worlds because of his truthfulness and sincerity.
rows.anchor: may peace and blessings be on Abraham (sws) in this world and in the next for his truthfulness and sincerity.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word salām is indefinite rather than bearing the definite article al, expressing its majesty.
rows.anchor: The word ٌم َلَاَس is not defined by the article ال to express its majesty.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase in this manner refers back to the peace and blessings of the previous verse and describes God’s treatment of sincere, befitting servants.
rows.anchor: The word َكِلَذَك in this manner) points to the peace and blessings mentioned in the previous verse.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believer here means a thorough believer; true faith has sincerity and completeness, and not every claimed faith is worthy before God.
rows.anchor: the essence of faith: it is one which has the spirit of sincerity and thoroughness in it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As a reward for passing the trial, Abraham received glad tidings of Isaac as a righteous prophet; that prophetic status, rather than another child, made the news significant.
rows.anchor: the Almighty gave Abraham (sws) the glad tidings of his second son – Isaac (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Torah reports Abraham saying that he wished Ishmael alone would continue to live in God’s presence, showing another son’s birth itself was no special glad tiding.
rows.anchor: he is reported to have said: “I wish only Ishmael continues to live in your presence.”

rows.speaker: The Jews
rows.claim: The Jews’ account identifies Isaac as the son Abraham offered for sacrifice.
rows.anchor: The story concocted by the Jews that it was Isaac (sws) who was offered for sacrifice

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author calls the Isaac-sacrifice account baseless: Isaac was born after the incident and was given as the reward for the sacrifice.
rows.anchor: He was born after the incident of sacrifice. He was not the one offered for sacrifice

rows.speaker: Those who regard this antecedent to be Abraham (sws)
rows.claim: The author rejects taking the pronoun’s antecedent as Abraham, calling that interpretation grossly mistaken.
rows.anchor: Those who regard this antecedent to be Abraham (sws) have grossly erred in their interpretation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun refers to Ishmael: if Abraham were intended, the verse would say his progeny, since Isaac is Abraham’s descendant rather than his parallel.
rows.anchor: This is because Isaac (sws) is not parallel to Abraham (sws) but from among his progeny.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God blessed Ishmael and Isaac, whose descendants multiplied; among them are sincere righteous believers and people who deviate into polytheism and disbelief.
rows.anchor: The progeny of both prospered and multiplied.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse reminds Israelites and Ishmaelites of their ancestors, the path they should follow, and how they have deviated.
rows.anchor: both the Ishmaelites and the Israelites are reminded at a very opportune time of their great ancestors

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this exegesis, conditional clauses may suppress their answer to convey an intensity that words cannot express.
rows.anchor: at times the answer to conditional clauses like this is suppressed and the intensity of the tone of the speaker is reflected by this suppression.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The suppressed answer in the example from Sūrah Zumar occurs after the believers draw near Paradise and its gates open.
rows.anchor: A clear example of this is coming up in Sūrah Zumar

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same suppression applies here because words cannot convey the intensity of the omitted answer.
rows.anchor: Similar is the case with the verse under discussion. Words are unable to express the intensity of the suppressed part.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The self-evident answer is that father and son became worthy of immense blessings by taking this step to please God.
rows.anchor: one should imagine how many great blessings of God they became worthy of.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Abraham, Moses and Aaron were the most celebrated messengers and pioneers of a great community whose law prevailed widely and for a long time.
rows.anchor: The most celebrated of messengers of God after Abraham (sws) were Moses (sws) and Aaron (sws) who became the pioneers of a great ummah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gave Moses and Aaron the guidance of the sharīʿah, freed them and the Israelites from Pharaoh’s slavery, and helped them triumph.
rows.anchor: the Almighty blessed Moses (sws) and Aaron (sws) with the guidance of the sharī‘ah and delivered them and their people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about helping them points specifically to Israel’s national victories after migrating from Egypt.
rows.anchor: The word ْمُاهَنْر َTصَن points to the triumphs notched up by the Israelites as a nation when they migrated from Egypt.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expressions for the clear book refer to the Torah; before it, no community received the sharīʿah in an organized clear book and people learned orally.
rows.anchor: They refer to the Torah. Before it, the Almighty never gave the sharī‘ah to any ummah in the form of a clear book.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Torah’s distinction is its organized, clear written form of the sharīʿah.
rows.anchor: The Torah has the distinction of being composed of the sharī‘ah in the form of an arranged and clear book.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the Torah was formally revealed to Moses alone, it is attributed to Aaron too because he was made Moses’s co-messenger.
rows.anchor: since Aaron (sws) was made a co-messenger with him the verse ascribes the Torah to Aaron (sws) as well.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God guided both messengers to the straight path; mentioning this also indirectly refutes Jewish accusations against Aaron.
rows.anchor: About both of them, it is stated that the Almighty guided them to the straight path.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These verses repeat material explained earlier: later people followed Moses and Aaron, God blessed them and humiliated their enemies, and He rewards sincere religious practice.
rows.anchor: after these two messengers, people continued to follow their ways; God sent His mercy and blessings on them and their enemies were humiliated

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People who follow their way today also merit God’s mercy; God will preserve their way, raise bearers of their message, and keep their name enduring.
rows.anchor: even if today there are such people, they too will be entitled to God’s mercy and blessings and God will grant permanence to their ways.
